evidence.label: A torsion-free hyperbolic group that is not residually finite

headline: A torsion-free hyperbolic group in which some element vanishes in every finite quotient.
scope: One finitely generated, torsion-free word-hyperbolic group built from a finite triangle complex. Lean covers non-residual-finiteness; the nonlinearity corollary is not a separate Lean conclusion.
plain: Hyperbolic groups are groups whose geometry bends like a saddle at large scales. A long-open question asked whether every such group can be fully seen through finite snapshots, called finite quotients. This paper proves no, with a Lean formalization listed: it builds a hyperbolic group with no elements of finite order where some element always disappears. It also claims the group has no faithful matrix model over any commutative field.
doesNot: This does not name which element always vanishes, and it does not address skew fields or infinite-dimensional representations.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Mikhail Gromov, whose theory of hyperbolic groups started the program behind the question
scorecard.significanceWhy: Whether every hyperbolic group is residually finite is a central open question in geometric group theory.

explanation:
Take the integers and the element 5. Reduce modulo 7, a finite group of seven clock positions. The number 5 lands on position 5, not on 0. So 5 survives in a finite image. Every nonzero integer n survives modulo |n| + 1, so the integers are residually finite. A group is residually finite when each nonidentity element has a nonidentity image in some finite group[1]. Such groups can be studied through finite snapshots.

A word-hyperbolic group is a finitely generated group whose distance graph has thin triangles. Every point on one side of a geodesic triangle lies near the other two sides[2]. Free groups are the standard example, and they are residually finite. Since Gromov's work in 1987, a central question asked whether every hyperbolic group is residually finite[2].

Several facts made this hard to test. Kapovich and Wise showed it is equivalent to every nontrivial hyperbolic group having a nontrivial finite quotient[3]. Agol showed hyperbolic groups acting nicely on cube complexes are virtually special, hence residually finite[4]. So a counterexample cannot have that cubical structure. Wise had groups that are not residually finite with nonpositive curvature, but they contain flat planes and are not hyperbolic[5].

The paper proves there is a torsion-free word-hyperbolic group that is not residually finite[6]. Torsion-free means no nonidentity element has finite order. The group comes from a finite complex of flat triangles glued along edges[7]. Hyperbolicity comes from a test on angles around each vertex. Consider equilateral triangles with 60° corners. Six around a point give 6 × 60° = 360°, which is flat. Seven give 420°, more than a full turn, which bends like a saddle. The criterion asks that every closed walk around a vertex have angle at least 2π + η, for some η > 0[8]. Then the group is torsion-free and hyperbolic[8].

The obstacle is to kill an element in all finite quotients at once. The paper uses a fixed finite family of four-edge "rectangular words." If each survived somewhere, a product of finite quotients would keep them all[14]. Then a rank count in matrices gives two incompatible bounds[14,9]. So one fixed member vanishes in every finite quotient, though the proof does not say which[10]. The paper also claims that every finite matrix representation, over any commutative field, kills that element[11].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof of a torsion-free hyperbolic group that is not residually finite. The Lean note says nonlinearity is not a separate conclusion there. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds, and the main theorem has a Lean formalization. The nonlinearity corollary is not a separate Lean conclusion. No specialist review is published.
